newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy crisis over Albania exposes govt fault line.
newsitem.headline: Italy crisis over Albania exposes govt fault line.

text.p: A dispute with far left allies over sending troops to Albania has starkly exposed a fault line in Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government which could eventually tear it apart.

Prodi has put his government's survival on the line over the next three days, calling confidence votes in the upper and lower houses of parliament after hard left ally Communist Refoundation opposed a plan to send an Italian-led multinational force to guard aid missions in Albania.

The mission was secured when centre-right opposition parties swung behind the government in parliament. In return they forced Prodi into a humiliating admission that his parliamentary majority had crumbled on a key foreign policy issue.

"The crisis over Albania has shown that there is not a real government majority," said Sergio Romano, a former diplomat who is now a leading political commentator. "This was always obvious but Prodi somehow managed to disguise it."

Prodi told the Senate, where his coalition government has an outright majority, that Communist Refoundation must be prepared to back his government's programme if it voted for him in a confidence vote scheduled for Thursday evening.
The Chamber of Deputies (lower house), where the government has to rely on the support of Refoundation's 34 deputies, will hold a similar vote on Saturday.

Refoundation pledged on Thursday to support Prodi, allowing him to live to fight another day. But his hastily patched up majority will be put to a severe test in the months ahead when the government unveils plans to prune a bloated welfare state.

Welfare reform is high on the agenda of a government that has taxed Italy's prosperous middle class until the pips squeak in a race to straighten out public finances and win a place in a planned European currency union.

With taxes biting ever deeper into the life-blood of the economy, the government has little option but to cut welfare spending if it is to bring about a lasting reduction in a heavy public sector deficit.
But Refoundation has nailed its colours to the mast as the defender of Italy's downtrodden and says it will fight any attempt to cut welfare and pension payments to the needy.
"On some policy issues there is clearly more divergence between Refoundation and the (government) majority than there is between the majority and the opposition," said Romano.

Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi seized on the government coalition's weakness in a parliamentary debate on Wednesday, saying his centre-right Freedom Alliance would consider backing a minority government provided Prodi ditched Refoundation.
Another challenge to the government will come at the end of the month when nine million Italians go to the polls in local elections in 1,100 towns and cities throughout the country.

Strains could also quickly resurface in the coalition if the Italian force in Albania suffers casualties. Refoundation has said it does not believe it is worth putting Italian lives at risk in Albania for what it sees as a neo-colonialist adventure.

Prodi, who has repeated doggedly that he wants to stay in office for a full five-year term, is now given only an even chance of surviving long enough to present a budget for 1998, something he wants to bring forward to mid-year.
"Unless the government gets the local elections and Albania right it won't last long enough for the budget," said Patrick McCarthy, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins university in Bologna.
"But there will be a lot of pressure on the Italian political class to allow Prodi a second budget," he added.
No government has stayed in office long enough to present two budgets in successive years since 1992, the year a corrupt political old guard was swept away in a fireball of scandal.
